title: Decimals with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)
header: Decimals with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

### Prerequisites

In previous texts, we learned how to represent numbers on the Soroban (算盤) and the Suanpan (算盤) (<htcite0>; <htcite1>), how to advance to higher numerical orders (families) while keeping the decimal marker (⚫) in the rightmost position (<htcite2>), and how to fill the spaces between the integers with decimal values (<htcite3>). We recommend studying them before you continue.

source.page: Higher orders with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
### Introduction

In all the abacus texts so far, the decimal marker (⚫) stayed in the same place: the rightmost position (<htcite0>; <htcite1>; <htcite2>). With the marker there, all nine columns of our abacus represent integer families: the rightmost column is the units, and the families grow to the left, up to the hundred millions.

However, the abacus of the *History Tracers* version hides a detail that we have not yet explored: the decimal marker (⚫) is not attached to the frame. It slides along a horizontal track in the middle of the columns. In this text, we will finally move it.

source.page: Higher orders with Soroban and Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
Reflection 1: Sliding...

Without moving a single bead, what do you think happens to the value shown on the abacus when we slide the decimal marker (⚫) to the left?

### Moving the marker

To move the decimal marker (⚫), place the pointer (or the finger, on touch screens) over it, press it, and drag it along the horizontal track that crosses the abacus in the middle. When you release it, the marker settles in the space between two columns.

The rule is simple: the columns to the left of the marker form the integer part, and the columns to the right form the fractional part (<htcite0>). With the marker in the rightmost position, no column remains to its right: every column is an integer column, and the value shown ends in “.0”. When we slide the marker one column to the left, the rightmost column stops counting units and starts counting tenths. Sliding it again creates a column of hundredths, and so on.

Let's see what the columns of our abacus represent when the marker is one column to the left of the rightmost position.

Table 1: Numerical orders (families) represented on the Soroban when the decimal marker (⚫) is one column to the left of the rightmost position.
Where: T. M. means ten million; H. Th., hundred thousand; T. Th., ten thousand; H., hundred; T., ten.

From **Table 1**, we can conclude that the position of the decimal marker (⚫) continues to indicate where the units are (<htcite0>). Every column to its left remains in the integer families, growing to the left exactly as before; every column to its right now represents fractional families, growing to the right: tenths, hundredths, thousandths...

In fact, every column changed family: the column that held the hundreds now holds the tens, the column that held the tens is now the units, and the former units column now counts tenths.

Notice also the “Value” field of the abacus: it now shows a point. The digits to the left of the point belong to the integer families, and the digits to the right of the point belong to the fractional families.

### Practicing with decimals

Time to practice! The abacus below is the same one we used in the previous texts (<htcite0>), but now we can drag its decimal marker (⚫). Follow the steps and keep an eye on the “Value” field.

🧮 Abacus:
⚫ Decimal marker

Practice 1: Sliding to the tenths...
In this practice, we will slide the decimal marker (⚫) and observe how the same beads change families.

1. Click the “Soroban (1x4)” button.
2. With the decimal marker (⚫) in the rightmost position, move the upper bead of the rightmost column. The value shown will be 5.0.
3. Now drag the decimal marker (⚫) one column to the left, without touching any bead. The value becomes 0.5: the same beads now represent five tenths.
4. Add two lower beads to the same rightmost column. The value becomes 0.7 — five tenths plus two tenths.
5. Click “⟳ Reset” and build the value 12.3: with the marker one column to the left of the rightmost position, move one lower bead in the third column from the right (the tens), two lower beads in the second column from the right (the units), and three lower beads in the rightmost column (the tenths).

Practice 2: Hundredths on the Suanpan...
Now we will create two fractional columns at once.

1. Click the “Suanpan (2x5)” button.
2. Drag the decimal marker (⚫) two columns to the left of the rightmost position. The two rightmost columns now represent the tenths and the hundredths.
3. In the rightmost column, move the upper bead and two lower beads. The value shows 0.07: seven hundredths. Notice the zero right after the point: the tenths column is empty, and its digit must still be shown.
4. In the tenths column, move three lower beads. The value becomes 0.37.
5. In the units column, move one lower bead. The value becomes 1.37.
6. To finish, drag the decimal marker (⚫) back to the rightmost position, without moving any bead. The value jumps to 137.0! The same beads now represent one hundred and thirty-seven units: only the marker decides which family each column belongs to.

In these practices, we observed that the beads never changed columns: it was the decimal marker (⚫) that changed the family of each column. That is why the same arrangement showed 1.37 with the marker to the left, and 137.0 with the marker in the rightmost position.

On the Suanpan (算盤), the alert about values greater than 9 continues to work in the same way (<htcite0>): each column, whether integer or fractional, must keep its digit between 0 and 9.

text.text:
### Conclusion

In this text, we learned that the decimal marker (⚫) of the Soroban (算盤) and the Suanpan (算盤) is not fixed: by sliding it along the horizontal track, we choose which columns represent integer families and which ones represent fractional families, such as the tenths and the hundredths.

With this, the abacus stops being a tool only for counting and becomes a tool for measuring: we can now represent on it decimal values of up to nine digits, exactly as we do with the Indo-Arabic numerals.

exercise_v2.question: When we slide the decimal marker (⚫) to the left, do the columns to its right start representing fractional families, such as the tenths and the hundredths?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: The marker separates the integer part, on its left, from the fractional part, on its right: the first column to the right of the marker represents the tenths, the next one the hundredths, and so on.

exercise_v2.question: When we slide the decimal marker (⚫), do the beads also need to change columns?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: The beads stay where they are: only the family of each column changes. The same beads that showed 1.37 show 137.0 when the marker returns to the rightmost position.
